title: The Movement Laws
subtitle: 'I don't have time for the gym' isn't the excuse you think.
law: The gym gets one hour. Your life gets the other fifteen. Win the fifteen.
intro:
"I can't lose weight, I don't have time for the gym." Babe, you sat for 14 hours today and moved from the bed to the desk to the couch. The gym was never the main problem.

You're not gonna like this, but for most people the gym isn't the big lever. The big lever is all the small moving you do the rest of the day. Walking to the car. Pacing on a call. Carrying laundry up the stairs. Scientists call it NEAT, which stands for non-exercise activity thermogenesis. You can call it 'moving without trying'.

NEAT can change a lot from person to person, and from day to day. Lean people often aren't training harder. They just sit less. They fidget, stand, walk and do stuff, without calling it a workout.

So here's what actually works: the lazy-girl version of fitness. No punishing cardio. No 'burning off' last night's pizza. Just small, sneaky ways to move more that fit the life you already have. Stack enough of them and your body quietly does the rest.

hacks.title: The NEAT Takeover
hacks.hook: Your daily steps can matter more than your workout. Yes, even that spin class.
hacks.callout: One hour at the gym, then 14 hours glued to a chair? That's not a routine, that's a cameo.
hacks.what: Stop thinking of movement as 'the workout' and start thinking of it as your whole day. Find your current daily step average, then raise it slowly. Small, boring movement all day beats one hard session followed by 10 hours on the sofa.
hacks.why: A well-known 1999 study in the journal Science, led by James Levine at the Mayo Clinic, overfed volunteers on purpose. The people who gained the least fat were the ones who naturally moved more in small ways, like fidgeting and standing. Daily movement adds up to far more than most people think, and it does not leave you wrecked or starving.
how: Check your phone or watch for your average steps over the last 7 days.
Add 1,000 steps to that number. That is your new daily target for the next 2 weeks.
Once it feels normal, add another 1,000. Keep going until you land around 7,000 to 10,000.
hacks.pro: Don't jump from 3,000 to 12,000 overnight. Slow raises stick. Big jumps burn you out by Thursday.

hacks.title: The 10-Minute Digestion Walk
hacks.hook: A 10-minute walk after eating can flatten your blood sugar spike. Timing is everything.
hacks.callout: Big dinner, straight to the couch, horizontal till bedtime? Your blood sugar would like a word.
hacks.what: Within 30 minutes of finishing your biggest meal, go for an easy 10-minute walk. No sweat, no speed. Just a stroll around the block, the office or even your hallway.
hacks.why: When you walk, your muscles pull sugar out of your blood to use as fuel. A 2022 review in the journal Sports Medicine found that even a few minutes of light walking after a meal lowered the blood sugar rise compared with sitting. Smaller spikes can mean fewer crashes and fewer 'I need something sweet' moments later.
how: Pick the meal you eat at home most often, usually dinner.
Put your shoes by the door before you sit down to eat.
When you finish, walk for 10 minutes before you touch the dishes or the couch.
Can't go out? Walk laps of your home or up and down the stairs.
hacks.pro: Turn it into a ritual with your partner, kid or dog. Nobody skips a walk when the dog is staring at them.

hacks.title: The Walk-and-Talk Law
hacks.hook: Every phone call is a free walk you're currently wasting on the couch.
hacks.callout: An hour-long call with your bestie, spent entirely lying down? That was a free walk, girl.
hacks.what: Make a rule: if you are on the phone and not looking at a screen, you are standing up and walking. Calls with mum, your best friend, customer service, voice notes. All of them are now walking time.
hacks.why: Most of us spend hours a week on calls while sitting still. A 20-minute call at an easy pace can easily be 2,000 steps or more. You are doing the call anyway, so the steps cost you zero extra time.
how: Buy or dig out a pair of wireless earbuds so walking feels easy.
The moment your phone rings, stand up before you answer.
Pace your room, your hallway or walk outside for the whole call.
For long work calls with no screen, book them as 'walking meetings' in your calendar.
hacks.pro: Stuck on hold with your bank? Perfect. That is the best cardio of your life.

hacks.title: The Stair Rule
hacks.hook: Two floors or less? The lift is not for you anymore.
hacks.callout: Waiting three minutes for the lift to go up one floor. Not me doing that daily.
hacks.what: Set a simple, non-negotiable rule: if it is two floors or less, you take the stairs. Up or down. No debate, no 'just today'. Rules beat decisions because you don't have to think.
hacks.why: Climbing stairs uses your biggest muscles, your glutes and thighs, so it takes much more effort than walking on flat ground. It is also great for shaping your legs and bum. And because it is a rule and not a choice, you never waste willpower arguing with yourself.
how: Decide your number right now: 'two floors or less, always stairs'.
At home, stop leaving things at the bottom of the stairs to 'take up later'. Take each thing up now.
At work or the mall, walk past the lift and look for the stair sign first.
Once two floors is easy, make it three.
hacks.pro: Going up more than your rule? Take the stairs for the last two floors only. Still counts.

hacks.title: Step Snacks
hacks.hook: You snack on food all day. Start snacking on steps instead.
hacks.callout: You'll get up for a snack every hour but not for a two-minute walk? Interesting.
hacks.what: A step snack is a tiny burst of movement, 2 to 5 minutes, sprinkled through your day. Every hour or so, you get up and walk, do a lap, climb a flight of stairs or march on the spot. Small bites, big total.
hacks.why: Long stretches of sitting keep your body in low-power mode. Short, regular breaks wake your muscles up and keep your daily movement ticking over. Ten step snacks of 3 minutes each is 30 minutes of walking, and you never had to 'find time'.
how: Set a quiet hourly reminder on your phone or watch from 9am to 5pm.
When it buzzes, stand up and move for 2 to 5 minutes. Refill water, walk to the far bathroom, do one flight of stairs.
Keep a tally on a sticky note. Aim for 8 step snacks a day.
hacks.pro: Feeling a craving? Take a step snack first. Often the craving was just boredom.

hacks.title: The Stand-to-Scroll Rule
hacks.hook: You're going to scroll anyway. Just stop doing it horizontal.
hacks.callout: Three hours of scrolling, zero steps, then 'I just don't have time to move'. Hmm.
hacks.what: Make one easy swap: when you open TikTok, Instagram or any feed just for fun, you stand up. Lean on the kitchen counter, pace, sway, stretch. Sitting is for work and meals. Scrolling is for standing.
hacks.why: Standing uses more energy than sitting because your leg and core muscles have to work to keep you upright. It also makes you fidget and shift, which adds more small movement. And a nice bonus: you will probably scroll for less time, because standing gets boring faster than lying on the couch.
how: Tell yourself the rule out loud once: 'Scrolling is a standing activity'.
Every time you catch yourself scrolling while sitting, stand up. No guilt, just stand.
Add small moves while you stand: calf raises, side steps or gentle squats during videos.
hacks.pro: Watching this brand's videos? Do 10 calf raises per video. You're welcome.

hacks.title: The Habit Hitchhike
hacks.hook: Glue tiny moves onto things you already do, and they happen on autopilot.
hacks.callout: You stand there staring at the microwave for two minutes anyway. Might as well do calf raises.
hacks.what: Pick habits you never miss, like brushing your teeth, boiling the kettle or waiting for the microwave. Attach one tiny move to each one. The old habit becomes the trigger for the new one.
hacks.why: New habits fail because you have to remember them. Habits you already have are automatic. When you hook a small move onto an automatic habit, you borrow its power. This is called habit stacking, and it works because the cue is already built into your day.
how: Write down 3 things you do every single day (for example: kettle, teeth, waiting for the shower to warm up).
Match each one with a tiny move: 10 squats while the kettle boils, calf raises while you brush, 20 wall push-ups while the shower warms up.
Use this sentence: 'After I ___, I will ___'. Stick it where the habit happens.
hacks.pro: Keep each move so small it feels silly. Silly and done beats impressive and skipped.

hacks.title: The Hungry Cardio Trap
hacks.hook: If intense cardio leaves you ready to eat the whole kitchen, it might be backfiring.
hacks.callout: Brutal cardio, then eating everything in sight because you 'earned it'? That's a trade, not progress.
hacks.what: Notice how you feel after long, hard cardio sessions. If you often want to eat the whole kitchen after, swap some of them for walking and strength training. Keep the moves that leave you feeling good, not starving.
hacks.why: Hard cardio burns energy, but for some people it also turns hunger way up and makes the sofa feel extra tempting for the rest of the day. That can cancel out the effort. Walking barely touches your appetite, and strength training helps build muscle, which shapes your body and supports your metabolism.
how: For the next 2 weeks, rate your hunger from 1 to 10 about an hour after each workout.
If hard cardio days are always a 8 or higher, swap 2 of those sessions for brisk walks.
Add 2 short strength sessions a week, even 20 minutes of squats, lunges and push-ups at home.
After any workout, eat a real meal with protein instead of 'rewarding' yourself with a treat.
hacks.pro: You don't need to 'earn' food with exercise, ever. Move to feel good, eat to fuel.

hacks.title: The Far-Side Parking Rule
hacks.hook: The best parking spot is the worst one. Stop circling like a shark.
hacks.callout: Circling the car park for ten minutes to save a 40-second walk. The irony, babe.
hacks.what: Stop circling for the closest spot. Park at the far end of the car park, get off the bus one stop early, or use the entrance that is furthest from where you need to go. Make distance the default.
hacks.why: Each far-away choice adds a few hundred steps. Do it at work, the supermarket and school pick-up, and you can add thousands of steps a week without planning a single walk. Bonus: far spots are easier to find, so you stop wasting time and stress hunting for a space.
how: Today, park in the row furthest from the door. Every trip, every time.
If you take the bus or train, get off one stop early on the way home at least 3 times a week.
In big stores or malls, walk the long way round to the thing you need.
hacks.pro: Use a shopping basket instead of a trolley when you only need a few things. Carrying adds work, and you buy less junk.

hacks.title: The Walking Pad Office
hacks.hook: Your Netflix habit could be walking you. One piece of kit, free steps.
hacks.callout: A whole season in one night, not one step taken. The couch is winning and it knows it.
hacks.what: A walking pad is a small, flat treadmill that slides under a standing desk or sits in front of your TV. You walk slowly, around 2 to 3 km per hour, while you answer emails, watch a show or scroll. Pair it with chores-as-movement on days you are home.
hacks.why: You are not trying to sweat. You are replacing sitting time with gentle walking time. One hour at a slow pace can add several thousand steps. It is one of the easiest ways for people with desk jobs to move more without taking time away from anything.
how: Start with just 20 to 30 minutes a day at a slow speed. Slow is the whole point.
Use it during low-focus tasks: emails, calls, Netflix, scrolling. Sit for deep work if you need to.
No walking pad yet? Turn chores into movement instead: put on 3 songs and speed-clean, carry laundry one load at a time, hand-wash the car.
hacks.pro: Wear proper trainers on the pad, not socks or slippers. Your feet and knees will thank you.

mythBust.myth: If you don't sweat, it doesn't count.
mythBust.truth: Sweat is just how your body cools down. It is not a score. Gentle, all-day movement like walking and standing often adds up to more than one intense workout, and it doesn't make you ravenous afterwards.

tryThis.title: Tonight's Try-This
tryThis.text: After dinner tonight, put your shoes on and take a 10-minute walk before you touch the dishes or the sofa. Put on one podcast episode or call a friend and just go.

journal: What are 3 things I do every day that I could glue a tiny move onto?
When during my day do I sit the longest without getting up?
Which kind of movement leaves me feeling energised, and which leaves me starving?
quote: You don't need a harder workout. You need a less glued-to-the-couch life.
